documents: Huang & Hawthorne (2022), Linking the scaling of tremor and slow slip near Parkfield, CA, Nature Communications 13:5826 (published PDF, 10 pages)
Publisher XML full text converted to located text (jats_text), g22_W4300861520.xml.txt
pages_convention: XML section and paragraph locators (jats_text); steps read off a figure cite the caption label as printed (Fig. N) with the PDF page counted from 1 in parentheses

entry.evidence: Here, we hypothesize that LFEs with a range of durations do exist: that we just need a more thorough approach to identify them.

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text), checked against the published PDF

steps.action: Pose the open question whether tremor (LFEs) and slow slip events are arrested by the same fault zone process or by two distinct ones, and frame it as a question of how LFE duration scales with moment.
steps.quote: we still debate whether tremor and slow slip are generated by the same process operating at different scales or by two distinct processes

steps.action: Take three rival moment-duration scalings from the literature: linear M0 ∝ T across slow earthquakes, moment-independent characteristic LFE durations, and cubic M0 ∝ T3 as for regular earthquakes.
steps.quote: Some found that LFE durations are independent of moment

steps.action: Compute Brune-type spectra under linear scaling to show that 2–8 Hz detection favours 0.2-s events, so a characteristic duration could be a detection bias.
steps.quote: we find that 0.2-sec-long events should be the easiest events to detect

steps.action: Hypothesize that LFEs with a range of durations exist and can be found with a more thorough search.
steps.quote: Here, we hypothesize that LFEs with a range of durations do exist: that we just need a more thorough approach to identify them.

steps.action: Build 0.2-s templates for families 37102 and 37140 by stacking Shelly's catalog detections, using the cited 0.2-s EGF duration of Thomas et al. They then make 0.1–0.6 s synthetic templates by Hann-window deconvolution and convolution, and run a multi-station matched filter over ~850 days, with stations CCRB and VARB held out.
steps.quote: We deconvolve the 0.2-sec templates with a 0.2-sec-long Hann-window source time function

steps.action: Run synthetic tests with low signal-to-noise ratios to check that durations can be resolved by averaging XCC over many channels: ~2% misclassification with 25 channels versus ~33% with one channel.
steps.quote: the durations are misclassified only ~2% of the time

steps.action: Detect 12,031 LFEs, each assigned a best-matching duration: 18% at 0.1 s and 23% at 0.3 s or longer. Longer LFEs are less often in Shelly's catalog.
steps.quote: We detect 12,031 LFEs in the ~850 days of data analyzed.

steps.action: Redo the detection in the 2–4 and 4–8 Hz bands and find that lower bands yield relatively more long events, as the spectral expectation predicts.
steps.quote: The ratio of long events to short events increases when we focus on lower frequencies

steps.action: Stack detections by duration at the held-out stations CCRB and VARB, cross-correlate the stacks with each duration's template, and bootstrap the stacks. The independent-station durations match the detection durations within about 0.05 s.
steps.quote: stacks from 0.2-sec detections most resemble a 0.2-sec template while 0.4-sec stacks most resemble a 0.4-sec template

steps.action: Check for alignment-induced bias with noise-corrected multi-taper spectra grouped by duration: longer groups have energy shifted to low frequencies. A Methods synthetic test shows that stacked noise-corrected spectra recover the signal even when noise power exceeds signal power.
steps.quote: the shift to low frequencies would not result from misaligned short ruptures

steps.action: Conclude that groups of LFEs with genuinely different durations at the same location have been established.
steps.quote: suggest that we have successfully identified groups of LFEs with different durations

steps.action: Measure station-median spectral power ratios (0.1-s/0.2-s and 0.4-s/0.2-s) to divide out site and path effects. The 0.4-s ratio falls and the 0.1-s ratio rises with frequency.
steps.quote: the 0.4-sec spectra are larger than the 0.2-sec spectra at low frequencies but become smaller than the 0.2-sec spectra at high frequencies

steps.action: Bootstrap the spectral ratios for uncertainty and compare them with noise-window spectral ratios as a reference. The noise ratios are flat with frequency.
steps.quote: The noise spectral ratios are almost constant with frequency; long-duration LFEs do not appear associated with long-period noise.

steps.action: Compute predicted spectral ratios for M0 ∝ T, M0 ∝ T3 and constant M0, with fall-off rates of 2 and 1, modelling the 0.1-s group with a 0.15-s prediction.
steps.quote: we compare our observations to predictions from different moment-duration relations

steps.action: Compare observed and predicted ratios. No prediction matches perfectly, but only linear scaling with γ = 2 reproduces the crossing of the short and long ratios.
steps.quote: But the prediction that best matches is the one with M0 ∝ T and γ = 2

steps.action: Stack unnormalized waveforms per duration, keep stacks with SNR > 5, and measure peak amplitudes normalized to the 0.2-s stack. Amplitudes are roughly independent of duration.
steps.quote: We find roughly duration-independent amplitudes

steps.action: Repeat the amplitude analysis in the 2–4 and 4–8 Hz bands and at the independent stations CCRB and VARB, obtaining similar amplitude ratios.
steps.quote: we obtain similar amplitude ratios when we redo our analysis in 2–4 Hz and 4–8 Hz frequency bands

steps.action: Map moment to amplitude with equal-moment synthetic LFEs, then predict amplitude-duration curves for linear, cubic and constant-moment scalings.
steps.quote: we generate moments and durations (0.1–0.6 s) following linear, cubic, and moment independent of duration scalings

steps.action: Compare the observed stack amplitudes with the three predicted curves: they agree with linear scaling and are inconsistent with cubic and constant-moment scaling.
steps.quote: the observed amplitudes agree well with the predictions from the linear moment-duration scaling, where M0 ∝ T, but are inconsistent with other scaling relations

steps.action: Run supplementary synthetic tests of how duration-dependent detectability could bias the amplitudes. No other moment distribution or scaling matches the stacks.
steps.quote: we do not find another moment distribution or moment-duration scaling that could match our stacks’ amplitudes

steps.action: Keep the claim that LFEs at the two families span 0.1–0.6 s in duration and that duration varies linearly with moment, for the average behaviour of stacked groups.
steps.quote: The identified groups of LFEs display a range of durations, and those durations vary linearly with moment.

steps.action: Reanalyze a published LFE dataset (ref. 17) in the supplement to show how uncertainties can bias an inferred scaling. They argue that earlier characteristic durations may reflect detection thresholds.
steps.quote: we reanalyze a published dataset17 and show how uncertainties could introduce bias in the inferred scaling

steps.action: Exclude near-source attenuation (path effects) as the cause of the LFEs' low-frequency content, because it would affect all LFEs at one location equally.
steps.quote: The varying frequency content cannot be created by a region at depth that attenuates high-frequency seismic waves

steps.action: Derive from M0 ∝ AD = A·Vslip·T and the observed scaling that slip rate is inversely proportional to rupture area.
steps.quote: that slip rates are inversely proportional to rupture areas

steps.action: Propose three rupture scenarios for longer LFEs: constant patch size, constant rupture speed, and constant stress drop.
steps.quote: And we may speculate about possible LFE rupture scenarios

steps.action: Place the LFE scaling on the cross-study linear trend from VLFEs, rapid tremor reversals and SSEs, and keep the inference that LFEs and SSEs share one fault zone process.
steps.quote: This simple scaling suggests that LFEs and slow slip events are generated by the same fault zone process: that LFEs are short slow slip events.

steps.action: Under the same-process hypothesis, discard the constant-patch and constant-speed scenarios and retain constant stress drop, as somewhat consistent with published stress drops.
steps.quote: we must discard constant-patch (Fig. 7a) and constant-speed (Fig. 7b) rupture scenarios

steps.action: Use size-dependent slip rates to exclude temperature-dependent arrest models (minimum asperity size, chemical reactions) and favour dilatant strengthening or brittle-viscous shear.
steps.quote: we could exclude models with temperature-dependent slip rates

Yes: M0 ∝ T, M0 ∝ T3, constant moment; also detection bias and path attenuation
Yes: distinct predicted spectral-ratio shapes and amplitude-duration curves
Found: natural LFEs of two Parkfield families in ~850 days of continuous data

tree.answer: Yes: thousands of repeating LFEs per family at the same patch
Yes: independent stations, frequency bands, spectra versus waveforms, synthetic misclassification and detection-bias tests
Linear scaling kept; cubic and constant-moment scaling and path effects excluded; a shared process with SSEs suggested
Not assessable: no review file supplied

end.claim: LFEs near Parkfield have durations of 0.1–0.6 s at the same location, and their stacked amplitudes and spectra follow linear moment-duration scaling (M0 ∝ T) rather than cubic or constant-moment scaling, the same scaling as slow slip events.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the synthetic variable-duration templates and multi-channel matched-filter classification, the shorter and longer LFE groups would not have been detected, so there would be no duration range to test the moment scaling on.

gates.evidence: The stated hypothesis that LFEs with a range of durations exist (§1 ¶4) directed the design of variable-duration templates and the search (§2.1 ¶2). The scaling claim faced spectral-ratio and amplitude comparisons in which cubic or constant-moment scaling could have won (§2.2 ¶1, ¶3). Only the held-out validation stations CCRB and VARB were fixed before detection (§2.1 ¶2). No hypothesis, threshold or analysis plan is said to have been fixed before the data were seen, and the 0.15-s substitution for the 0.1-s prediction was chosen 'to allow a better match' (§2.2 ¶1).

imports.item: bootstrap resampling for confidence bounds on durations, spectral ratios and amplitudes
matched-filter (template cross-correlation) detection with median-absolute-deviation threshold

novelty_claims.quote: Our results show varying durations (0.1–0.6 s) and spectra for LFEs at the same location.
Our detection approach is able to find more long (~0.4 s) LFEs than previous studies in Parkfield
Our observed LFEs provide one more piece of the slow earthquake spectrum.

limits:
Only the published paper and its XML text were supplied. The peer-review file is absent, although the paper thanks named referees (Honn Kao, David Shelly) (PDF p. 10), so no review sequence can be coded and question 9 is unanswered. The supplementary material was not supplied: the detection-bias synthetic tests (Supplementary Figs. 12–19), the reanalysis of ref. 17 (Supplementary Figs. 20–22), the frequency-band tests and the independent-station amplitudes are coded from their main-text descriptions only. Code is available only on request (§4 Code availability), so reproduction is not possible from the paper.

Sub-claim statuses:
- That durations vary at one location and so reflect source, not path, is confirmed against the attenuation rival (§3 ¶3).
- That LFEs and SSEs share one fault zone process is best_explanation, inferred from a cross-study trend (Fig. 1a) that is not tested here (§3 ¶6).
- Vslip ∝ A^-1 is a derivation from the scaling, not an observation (§3 ¶4).
- The preference for the constant-stress-drop scenario and for dilatant or brittle-viscous mechanisms is best_explanation at most; the authors call the scenarios 'very simplistic hypotheses' (§3 ¶7).
- That prior characteristic durations reflect detection thresholds is a suggestion, best_explanation (§3 ¶2).

The scaling rests on stacked group averages for two families over 0.1–0.6 s (§3 ¶1), so it is a result within a narrow range. Spectral predictions did not match perfectly, and the 0.1-s group was modelled with a 0.15-s prediction to improve the fit (§2.2 ¶1). Inference: this is a post hoc adjustment, coded inside step 14 rather than as a return_after_failure because the text does not report a failed first attempt.

The composition is coded strong_inference because the three scaling rivals share two crucial comparisons that exclude two of them. However, the conditions were found, not set, and the walk also has capability_first features (the new template method precedes the observation).

disagreements.target: Studies reporting characteristic, moment-independent LFE durations near Parkfield, in Cascadia and in Mexico (refs 14–16, 47)
disagreements.support: Frequency-band-dependent detections and the detection of longer and shorter LFEs suggest that characteristic durations arise from the 2–8 Hz observation band and thresholding.
disagreements.quote: could reflect observational capability and thresholding, not a physical property of tremor

disagreements.target: Supino et al. 2020, self-similar (M0 ∝ T3) LFE scaling (ref. 17)
disagreements.support: A supplementary reanalysis of their published dataset shows how data uncertainties could bias the inferred scaling.
disagreements.quote: we reanalyze a published dataset17 and show how uncertainties could introduce bias in the inferred scaling

disagreements.target: Studies finding LFE or SSE durations scaling as M0^1/3, like regular earthquakes (refs 17, 32–34)
disagreements.support: For the Parkfield LFEs, observed stack amplitudes and spectral ratios match linear scaling and are inconsistent with M0 ∝ T3; SSE scaling is not retested.
disagreements.quote: but are inconsistent with other scaling relations

disagreements.target: Explanations of LFE low-frequency content by near-source attenuation (refs 48–50)
disagreements.support: Durations and frequency content vary among LFEs at the same location, which a fixed attenuating region could not produce.
disagreements.quote: [...] that region would attenuate all LFEs in a given location in the same way

disagreements.target: Slow-earthquake arrest models with temperature-dependent slip rates: minimum asperity size (ref. 20), chemical reactions (ref. 27)
disagreements.support: Linear scaling implies size-dependent slip rates, and temperature is unlikely to vary systematically with fault size.
disagreements.quote: as the temperature is unlikely to vary systematically with fault size

disagreements.support: The variable-duration search adds events, especially long-duration LFEs, that the catalog missed.
disagreements.quote: Longer LFEs are less likely to be in Shelly’s catalog7
